HydraCompletion, in plain terms

A study of the internal signals an AI reasoning model uses to decide “I’m done thinking — here’s my answer.”

Paper title: “When Correctness Cannot Be Measured”

1 · What this is

Modern AI systems can think longer on harder problems — looping an internal reasoning step again and again. But something has to decide when to stop. That decision is handed to an internal “completion signal”: the model’s confidence, whether its answer has stopped changing, a learned “halting” switch, or how much its internal state is still moving.

Everyone assumes these signals tell you whether the reasoning finished correctly. This project asks the sharper question: can we even measure whether that assumption is true? — and finds a hidden trap where the answer is “no,” while all the numbers still look perfectly healthy.

2 · The setup — a stopping rule

Input
A hard problem
→
Think
Loop the reasoning step k times
→
Signal asks
“Am I done & correct?”
→
Output
Stop & answer

The whole question is whether that third box — the completion signal — is trustworthy.

3 · The discovery — the measurement can silently break

To test a signal you correlate it with correctness (a score called AUROC: 0.5 = useless, 1.0 = perfect). “Correct” just means the model’s output matched the target answer. Here’s the trap:

Push past training depth
Ask for more reasoning than it ever learned
→
Collapse
Output freezes to one constant answer
→
“Correct” now means…
did the label happen to equal that constant?
correct  ⇔  label = c   ⟹   AUROC(signal → correctness)  =  AUROC(signal → the data label)

Once the output is constant, correctness stops being a property of the model’s thinking and becomes a property of the data. Any signal that tracks task structure now impersonates a correctness detector — with a random sign that flips seed to seed.

What it looks like on the surface

  • Accuracy near chance → looks like a “hard but informative” problem
  • AUROC numbers far from 0.5 → look meaningful and confident
  • Nothing throws an error or a warning

What is actually happening

  • The correctness endpoint is unevaluable, not just noisy
  • Their real run: score swung 0.095 → 0.991 across random seeds
  • That “instability” was the arbitrary sign of an artifact, not a real signal

They caught this the honest way: a pre-registered experiment returned a No-Go (3 of 5 seeds), recorded unchanged — and diagnosing why revealed the trap. They then found the exact same collapse in a second, unrelated task & architecture, so it isn’t a quirk of one model.

4 · What was done about it

BUILD 01

A non-degeneracy gate

A checklist run before any correctness score is computed: is the output varied enough (predicted-positive fraction 0.2–0.8), both answer classes present, enough correct & incorrect states? If a cell fails, it’s excluded and reported — never quietly patched.

BUILD 02

A benchmark with real depth

Graph reachability, where each reasoning loop is exactly one hop of message passing. So “not enough thinking” becomes a hard mathematical bound — the answer cannot arrive before d(s,t) steps — instead of a guess.

BUILD 03

A locked-down protocol

train 15 fresh seeds→ verify checkpoints→ calibrate depth→ 🔒 freeze choices→ human review→ evaluate

Pre-registered in advance. The calibration file is written read-only and the code refuses to overwrite it — so “we didn’t peek” is enforced by the filesystem, not a promise. Git history keeps the full trail, including a retracted claim.

BUILD 04

A fair test of 5 stopping signals

Re-ran the whole study on 15 new seeds (13 valid), one score per seed, with bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds — never pooling states, which would hide the seed-to-seed spread that started this whole thing.

5 · The verdict — which signal actually knows if it’s right?

Completion signalCorrectness AUROCVerdictWhy
Answer stability
0.921		 Robust ✓ Passes every criterion setting tested
Fixed-point residual (rFP)
0.731		 Borderline Works only at the pre-set threshold; fragile
Confidence / entropy
0.820*		 Fails Predicts the label (1.000), not correctness — a confound
Learned halting head
0.109		 Anti-predictive Below chance — it fires most confidently when the model is wrong

Bar shows AUROC from 0 to 1; the grey line is chance (0.5). *Confidence’s score is real but is mostly detecting the answer itself, so it’s disqualified by the label-confound check. (A supervised “probe” scored a perfect 1.000 but was excluded — it needs the very labels it’s meant to detect and doesn’t transfer across depth.)

6 · How it can be used

🧪
As a safety check for any evaluation

Before claiming “signal X predicts correctness,” run the non-degeneracy gate first. If the output has collapsed, the number is meaningless no matter how good it looks. This applies to any study that derives “correct” by comparing a model output to a target.

⚙️
Practical guidance for adaptive-compute systems

If you’re building a model that decides when to stop thinking: prefer answer stability as the stopping signal, be skeptical of raw confidence, and don’t trust a learned halting head blindly — here it halted most on the wrong answers.

📊
As a testbed

The interface-enforced-depth reachability benchmark is a clean playground for adaptive-computation, halting, and depth-extrapolation research, because “insufficient reasoning” has an exact, verifiable meaning.

📐
As a template for rigorous ML research

Pre-registration, an amendment made before data, frozen read-only artifacts, a human-review gate, a recorded No-Go, a retracted claim, and full git provenance — a worked example of honest, reproducible practice.

One-sentence takeaway: Before asking whether an internal signal predicts correctness, first check that correctness is still measurable — because when a model’s output collapses to a constant, the usual metrics keep producing confident numbers that mean nothing.

Source folder: HydraCompletion-Research · documents read: README.md, main.tex (paper), TASK2_SPEC.md, EXECUTION_LOG.md.

Speech AI Model Plan - 2 x RTX 6000 Ada 48GB
Updated: 18 Jun 2026
Page 1
 Speech AI Model Selection and Training Plan
 For your 30 lakh INR server: 2 x NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada 48GB GPUs, Threadripper PRO 9975WX, 256GB ECC RAM
 Focus domains: Speech-to-Text (STT), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and the LLM layer used inside voice agents
 Decision
 Recommendation
Best production architecture
Use a modular pipeline first: STT -> LLM -> TTS. It is easier to debug, fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy than end-to-end S2S.
Best Indian-language LLM layer
Sarvam-30B-FP8 for Indian-language voice agents and transcript reasoning; use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as a strong general reasoning/coding backup.
Best STT starting point
Indian languages: IndicConformer 600M + Whisper large-v3-turbo fallback. English/realtime: Canary-Qwen, Parakeet v3, Voxtral Mini Realtime, or Higgs Audio v3 STT.
Best TTS starting point
Indian languages: IndicF5 or Indic Parler-TTS. General/custom voice research: F5-TTS, Qwen3-TTS, Fun-CosyVoice3, Higgs Audio v3 TTS, ZONOS2, Dia.
Can train from scratch?
Yes for small/medium ASR and TTS models. No for modern 7B+ LLMs, 30B+ MoE models, large omni models, or foundation-grade multilingual TTS/STT from scratch on only 2 GPUs.
Main fine-tuning strategy
Use full fine-tuning for small/medium ASR/TTS when VRAM allows; use LoRA/QLoRA/PEFT for LLMs and speech-LLMs; use FSDP/DeepSpeed only when necessary.
 Label
 Meaning
Run
The model can be used for inference on your server.
Fine-tune
You can adapt an existing pretrained model to your data. For big models this usually means LoRA/QLoRA/adapters.
Train from scratch
Start from random weights and train the model yourself. This needs far more data and compute than fine-tuning.
YES
Practical on your 2 x 48GB GPU server if you have enough clean data.
LIMITED
Possible for research or smaller variants, but not recommended for production-quality foundation models.
NO
Not practical from scratch on this server; use a pretrained checkpoint and fine-tune/adapt it.

8. Practical Rules
●
Do not spend months training a large LLM or omni speech model from scratch on this server. Use pretrained weights and LoRA/QLoRA.
●
Spend your training budget first on STT fine-tuning. Domain audio, local accents, noisy phones, and vocabulary give the biggest accuracy gains.
●
For TTS, collect clean, consented voice data. Never clone or imitate a real person's voice without permission.
●
Train from scratch only for focused ASR/TTS components where you control the data and evaluation set.
●
Evaluate models with real user audio, not only public benchmarks. Track WER/CER, latency, GPU memory, hallucinations, pronunciation errors, and subjective voice quality.
